gradcam: Grad-CAM heatmaps on representative test images (2 correct-benign, 2 correct-malignant, 2 false-positive, 2 false-negative) show the CNN attending to dense nuclear/tissue regions in malignant cases, consistent with plausible tissue-level visual cues. This is descriptive, not proof of medically correct reasoning.
attention: In the visualized test group (131 images), attention weights were highly concentrated on a small subset of images (top-5 images held ~35% of total weight combined), with a long tail of low-weight images. This indicates the attention model is selectively weighting certain images more heavily rather than averaging uniformly -- but this reflects the model's learned internal weighting, not confirmed biological importance.
evaluation: A full audit of CNN test metrics against saved Day-2 results showed an exact match (AUROC/F1/Accuracy), confirming reproducibility of the reported baseline.
robustness: The CNN baseline was fairly robust to mild Gaussian noise (AUROC drop of 0.003, from 0.9062 to 0.9032). It was more sensitive to Gaussian blur (AUROC drop of 0.035, to 0.8713), with a shift toward predicting malignant more often (sensitivity/F1 increased, specificity decreased). This suggests image sharpness/focus quality could meaningfully affect predictions in deployment-like conditions, and is a legitimate limitation to disclose.
limitations: Grad-CAM and attention visualizations show model behavior, not ground-truth correctness. Only the CNN pathway was visualized with Grad-CAM; the DINOv2/Foundation pathway was not (documented limitation). Robustness testing covered only 2 perturbation types on the CNN model, not the full model suite. No clinical validation, diagnostic deployment readiness, or biological causality is claimed from any of these results.
